Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
constantly scan environment for signs of threat
make sure to stay close to exit

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Negative Appraisals.value: The people responsible have faced no consequences
The world is a dangerous place
People are not what they seem

issues.item: Tactile (Restrained): Feeling physically restrained or held down
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'feeling physically restrained or held down' implies a hands-on assault/restraint context that is not supported by the rest of the profile. The other trigger, threat, and appraisal items consistently describe ongoing danger/hypervigilance related to being followed or encountered, making this tactile restraint trigger clinically discordant with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically to stop thinking about the event is not well supported by the rest of the selected profile. The formulation and items emphasize hypervigilance, danger appraisals, and place/proximity avoidance, but there are no memory/intrusion items or other indicators of overwhelming internal re-experiencing that would make this strategy fit coherently here. It reads as a symptom-management strategy for a different presentation than the one otherwise described.

'Drug Use' is the only clearly incoherent item in the selected five components. The rest of the profile forms a coherent stalking-related pattern: triggers of proximity/being followed/bicycle plausibly cue threat; threat items reflect hypervigilance and false alarms; negative appraisals center on danger, distrust, and lack of justice; and checking surroundings/avoiding location plausibly follow from those appraisals and threat beliefs. In contrast, drug use is not supported by the rest of the selected content: there are no accompanying items indicating broader emotion-regulation coping, dissociative distress, sleep-related self-medication, or generalized avoidance that would make substance use a clinically grounded strategy here. Given the formulation, Maladaptive Strategies is strongly linked from Threat and moderately from Negative Appraisals, so selected strategies should plausibly arise from the expressed threat beliefs/appraisals. 'Drug Use' feels disconnected from the otherwise specific hypervigilant stalking profile and is the only item that clinicians would be likely to question as belonging to the same coherent self-report pattern.

vignette:
Madeleine is a 33-year-old graphic designer of Dutch descent who lives with her husband in a mid-sized Pacific Northwest city. She presented for therapy approximately eight months after a prolonged stalking experience that began, by her account, as something she initially dismissed as coincidence. A man she had briefly encountered through a neighbourhood cycling group began appearing with unsettling regularity - outside the coffee shop where she worked remotely on Tuesdays, on the same bike path she used for her morning commute, idling near the entrance to the studio building where her design firm leased a shared workspace. The encounters escalated over several months: notes left on her bicycle, which she locked outside the studio; a direct confrontation on a quiet residential street during which he stood close enough that she could smell his jacket. She described the moment of that confrontation as the point at which something shifted permanently in her understanding of safety. He was never more than two feet from her, blocking the narrow pavement, and she had nowhere to go. She reported the situation to police, but no charges were filed, and the man eventually ceased contact without legal consequence.

In the weeks that followed, Madeleine found that the world she had moved through easily before felt structurally altered. The bicycle she had ridden to work every day since graduate school sat untouched in her hallway. She had come to associate it not merely with the stalking itself but with the particular vulnerability of being in motion, exposed, trackable - a feeling she could not separate from the machine that had once been ordinary. She stopped using the bike path entirely and began taking rideshares to the studio, though she later stopped going to the studio at all, shifting to working from home. The shared workspace, located two blocks from where the confrontation had occurred, was a place she was certain she could not enter without scanning every face and every doorway, and she found that the mental effort of doing so made sustained creative work impossible. Her output slowed. A client she had worked with for three years quietly moved their account elsewhere after she missed two consecutive deadlines.

At home and in public, Madeleine's attention had reorganised itself around threat. She described entering any room - a grocery store, her husband's family gatherings, even her own living room when the blinds were open - with an immediate, involuntary survey of where the exits were. She positioned herself accordingly, always with a wall at her back and a clear path to a door. She was not fully conscious of doing this until her husband pointed it out at a restaurant, and she found she could not explain it to him in a way that felt adequate. She was often startled by sounds that she recognised, intellectually, as harmless - a door closing in another room, footsteps behind her on a footpath - and her body responded before her reasoning could intervene. She had come to believe that this was simply accurate perception, that the world genuinely contained dangers that others were naively blind to, and that people in general were capable of concealing intentions that bore no resemblance to their surface presentation.

What weighed on her most persistently was the absence of any formal resolution. The man who had followed her had faced no legal consequence, and she was certain this meant that nothing protected her from it happening again. She had come to feel that the systems she might once have trusted to enforce accountability were indifferent to what she had experienced. This conviction had begun to colour her marriage in ways she found difficult to articulate - not distrust of her husband specifically, but a generalised wariness that she described as a glass wall between herself and other people.

Madeleine sought therapy after her husband gently observed that she had not left their neighbourhood in six weeks. She came to the intake session having identified an exit from the waiting room before sitting down. What she said she most hoped for was to ride her bicycle to work again. What she was most afraid of was that she no longer trusted herself to know when she was actually safe.
